levelMapping: L2 ≈ Google L4 / Meta E4 / Amazon SDE II; 2–5 YOE, title is just 'Software Engineer'. L1 = new grad / 0–2 YOE (early-career postings cap experience at ~18 months). L3 ≈ Google L5 (senior scope, no 'Senior' title). Stripe calibrates level inside the loop — the System Design round is what separates L2 from L1 — so with ~3.3 YOE expect L2 but confirm the target level with the recruiter before the onsite is scheduled.

process.summary: Stripe does not run LeetCode-style rounds. Every coding round is a long, story-driven, multi-part 'practical' problem (parse → apply business rules → extend) where you must write and run your own tests, and parts unlock one at a time. The 2025–26 loop for an experienced hire is: recruiter screen → (often) 60-min HackerRank OA → 60-min live technical 'team screen' → virtual onsite of 4–5 rounds: Programming exercise, Bug Squash (debug a real open-source library), Integration (build against an API/spec in a provided repo), System Design (L2 and above), Hiring Manager/behavioral. Since spring 2026 many loops add an 'AI programming exercise' on HackerRank with an embedded assistant (Claude Opus / Gemini Flash). Grading is strict on completing parts (2 of 3 is the usual bar), readable production-style code, and narrated reasoning; interviewers rate strong-yes/weak-yes/weak-no/strong-no and a single weak-no usually ends the loop.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.what: Background, motivation, level fit, logistics; recruiter notes are forwarded to later interviewers.
rounds.probes: A product-specific 'why Stripe' (APIs, developer experience), tech stack, current comp/level expectations, location (Bengaluru vs remote).

rounds.name: HackerRank online assessment
rounds.what: One long practical problem in 3–5 parts; each part unlocks only after the previous one passes its tests. Implementation-heavy (parsing, maps/sets, business rules), not DP/graphs. Web IDE with print-debugging only; AI tools forbidden; tab/window activity logged. Often skipped for referrals/experienced hires, standard for new grad and India/university applications.
rounds.probes: Correct handling of boundary cases in hidden tests; modular code so later parts reuse earlier functions; speed — candidates consistently call it 'super lengthy'.

rounds.name: Technical phone screen / team screen
rounds.what: Live pair-programming on CoderPad or your own IDE (screen-shared) in any language. One multi-part problem (typically 3–4 parts: reconciliation, shipping-cost tiers, accept-language parsing, fraud rules, KYC validation, task tree, linked merchants). You must write test cases and get them running against provided examples.
rounds.probes: Clarifying questions on ambiguous specs, readable naming/helper functions over micro-optimisation, backward compatibility (earlier tests still pass after extending), edge cases you raise unprompted, pace — finishing ≥2 parts cleanly is the usual bar; ≥3 is safe.

rounds.name: Onsite: Programming exercise
rounds.what: Same format as the screen but harder/longer: email-subscription scheduler, account balances with rejections and platform overdraft, transaction fees, rules evaluation. Often needs heaps/sorting by time plus careful state handling.
rounds.probes: Sort by parsed timestamps not strings, ordering ties, integer cents over floats, re-running earlier parts' tests after adding a part, stating complexity for what you actually wrote.

rounds.name: Onsite: Bug Squash
rounds.what: You get a local checkout of a real open-source library with 2–3 planted bugs (from real GitHub issues) and failing tests; find, explain and fix them in your IDE while screen-sharing. Repos by language: Python → Mako templating (most common) or python-requests (redirect body replay); Java → SnakeYAML or Jackson-core; JS → unnamed libraries (React async-fetch race reported); C++ → yaml-cpp; Kotlin/Java → Moshi (Square). Docs/StackOverflow allowed; AI tools not.
rounds.probes: Systematic debugging: reproduce, run a single failing test, breakpoints in a real debugger (print-debugging is penalised), reading stack traces, avoiding rabbit holes, defending that the fix addresses root cause not just the test. 2 of 3 bugs fixed is reported as passing; interviewers give almost no help.

rounds.name: Onsite: Integration
rounds.what: Clone a private repo with a README/GitHub-issue style spec and long API docs; implement a small feature end to end: read JSON/GeoJSON files, make authenticated HTTP requests (POST JSON, save a returned PNG), parse responses, write files. Canonical tasks: 'Bikemap' (5 tasks), HTTP request replayer with dynamic IDs, duplicate-request tracker, contacts-API enrichment, paginated sync. Internet allowed, no AI. Senior variants hit the real Stripe API.
rounds.probes: Reading unfamiliar docs fast, knowing your HTTP client/JSON/file-IO syntax by heart, lng/lat ordering, binary file writes, error handling at the API boundary, adapting when the interviewer changes requirements mid-round. Most candidates finish ~3 of 5 parts; finishing all parts was cited as a hard requirement in at least one rejection.

rounds.name: Onsite: AI programming exercise (2026)
rounds.what: HackerRank sandbox with an embedded AI chat (Claude Opus or Gemini Flash reported; Gemini Flash is faster). Standard prompt: parse accept/block rules with `if` conditions over a list of transactions, building up to nested AND/OR logic, from a detailed README. You are expected to lean on the AI (read README → plan → generate → you review, add tests, run).
rounds.probes: Why you trust (or don't) the generated code, edge cases the AI missed, meaningful tests, catching over-engineering, explaining every decision. Candidates who hand-write everything are asked why they aren't using the AI; those who accept blindly are asked why they trust it.

rounds.name: Onsite: System design
rounds.what: Only for L2 and above (new-grad loops skip it). Payments-flavoured prompts: ledger/bookkeeping service, webhook delivery, metrics counter, rate limiter, idempotent payment API, recurring-payment scheduler; occasionally generic (URL shortener, Twitter, tracing). Diagramming in a shared tool (Whimsical/Excalidraw), no coding.
rounds.probes: Idempotency raised unprompted, consistency vs availability for money movement, hot-account contention, exactly-once vs at-least-once + dedupe, retries/backoff/DLQ, failure modes ('where does it break first'), API shape and misuse, monitoring/rollout. Interviewers interject throughout and note whether they had to redirect you.

rounds.name: Hiring manager / behavioral
rounds.what: STAR-style conversation mapped to Stripe's operating principles: biggest project and how work was divided, ownership, conflict with a peer/manager, a time your voice wasn't heard, learning from a mistake, setting deadlines, why Stripe. Also used for team matching; HM-round candidates are reportedly stack-ranked in ~2-week windows.
rounds.probes: Candour about failures, product/user thinking after an MVP, how you work under unclear requirements, written/verbal clarity. Reported as a real elimination point, not a formality.

process.indiaNotes: Stripe hires engineers into its Bengaluru office at L1 (new grad/intern conversions) and L2+ (experienced), and the loop is the same global format — no DSA-only rounds and no India-specific 'machine coding'. Reported Bengaluru loops (Dec 2024 new grad offer; 2025–26 interns; Sep 2026 full-time): HackerRank OA → 60-min team screen (2 practical questions) → onsite with Programming exercise + Debugging (bug squash) and/or Integration → Hiring Manager chat; a Sep 2026 Bengaluru full-time report had OA → coding → AI-assisted coding + bug fixing → HM. Interns get 2 technical rounds (programming + integration) and no bug squash; new grads get bug squash and no system design; L2 gets system design. India online applications sometimes get a HackerRank screen that includes MCQs plus coding. Interviewers may be in Bengaluru, Singapore or the US, so slots can be early morning/late evening IST. Experienced-hire Bengaluru reports are thinner than US ones; the question bank (reconciliation, email scheduler, Bikemap, Mako, rules parser) is shared globally.
process.timeline: 4–8 weeks end to end for experienced hires (OA invite ~2–5 days after applying; screen ~1–2 weeks later; onsite 1–3 weeks after the screen, usually one day of back-to-back virtual rounds; HM chat a few days later; decision within ~1 week, sometimes 2–3 weeks when stack-ranked). Intern/new-grad cycles in Bengaluru ran ~2 months.
tips: Practise the exact multi-part format: build Part 1 as small reusable functions so Parts 2–4 extend rather than rewrite; re-run earlier tests after every part.
Write tests from the first minute (unittest/pytest, JUnit, or hand-rolled asserts) — 'use tests to demonstrate correctness' is in nearly every prompt and is graded.
Read the whole spec before typing; most reported failures were from skimming a long prompt (fee rules, rule parser) and missing edge cases, not from algorithmic difficulty.
Use Python (or JS) unless you are faster in something else — Java boilerplate (getters/constructors) cost multiple candidates a part; C++ is explicitly discouraged by recruiters.

For Bug Squash, rehearse on the actual public repos: clone Mako (ast.py, codegen.py, lookup.py) and python-requests, run `pytest` on a single test, and practise breakpoints in your IDE — print debugging was cited in a rejection. Verify your Python/JDK version matches the provided repo before the day.

For Integration, memorise your HTTP client (requests.post with json=, saving response.content in 'wb'), json/csv/file IO, and GeoJSON [lng, lat] ordering; practise reading long API docs under a timer.
Treat partial credit as real: 2 of 3 parts cleanly tested beats 3 parts with a bug; say out loud when an approach stops working (e.g., greedy breaks under a new constraint) and switch explicitly.
Ask clarifying questions even when the interviewer says 'I don't know' — the rubric rewards stating assumptions; several rejections cited not confirming requirements.
Have a backup internet connection and a working local dev setup; audio/debugger failures mid-round have cost candidates offers.
Prepare 6–8 STAR stories mapped to Stripe operating principles (users first, craft, urgency, collaboration without ego) — the HM round eliminates people who passed every technical round.
process.notes: No DSA/LeetCode round; the LC-tagged Stripe list is small and mostly reflects practical problems people mapped to LC afterwards. OA platform: HackerRank (also hosts the AI-assisted round). Coding screens use CoderPad or your own IDE; onsite coding rounds are screen-shared in your IDE. Language is free choice (interviewer matched to your language); Ruby is Stripe's stack but not required. Cool-off: ~6 months after a screen/code-pair rejection (Blind), 12 months after an onsite or OA failure (recruiter-stated in a Sep 2026 report; some teams invite earlier re-apply). Levels: L1–L3 'Software Engineer', L4+ 'Staff'; new-grad loops drop system design; senior loops may add API design. Debrief: interviewers vote strong/weak yes/no; a hire needs ≥2–3 strong yes and nothing below weak yes. AI assistants are forbidden in OA, screen, bug squash and integration; permitted only in the dedicated AI round.

dsa.title: Currency conversion over exchange-rate graph (Evaluate Division)
dsa.variant: Stripe version is a 3–4 part phone-screen problem on a rates string like 'AUD:USD:0.7,AUD:JPY:100,USD:CAD:1.2' (rates usable in both directions). Part 1: parse and return a direct rate (-1 if none). Part 2: allow exactly one intermediate currency. Part 3: pick the best rate (max product) among paths, or the path with fewest hops (BFS) — confirm which 'best' means. Part 4: any number of hops / return all computable rates; return route + effective rate + converted amount rounded to 2 dp.
dsa.evidence: Reported on Glassdoor (Senior SWE), a 2021 write-up, two GitHub prompt collections, Aced's 2026 guide lists it among first-round problems, InterviewDB lists 'Currency Conversion' phone screen last reported ~2026-08.

dsa.title: Shipping routes: direct cost → one-transfer route → cheapest route (Cheapest Flights Within K Stops)
dsa.variant: Input string such as 'US:UK:FEDEX:5,US:CA:UPS:1,CA:FR:DHL:3,UK:FR:DHL:2' (or comma/colon swapped). Part 1: travelCost(src, dst, method) → 5. Part 2: travelRoute(src, dst) with at most one intermediate country, returning {path, methods, cost} (any route is fine). Part 3: cheapest such route. Part 4 (rarely reached): allow multiple intermediates → BFS/Dijkstra. Interviewer probes empty strings, missing countries, output shape (string vs object).
dsa.evidence: LeetCode Discuss phone-screen post, Ziheng-Qi repo (two reports), InterviewDB 'Shipping Route' phone screen last reported ~2026-04.

dsa.title: Brace expansion (3 parts)
dsa.variant: Part 1: expand a single brace group with prefix/suffix, e.g. '/2022/{jan,feb,march}/report' → three paths. Part 2: invalid inputs — fewer than 2 tokens inside braces ('pre{mid}suf', 'pre{}suf'), missing/unbalanced or reversed braces → return the input unchanged. Part 3: multiple/nested groups = LC 1087 (usually only discussed).
dsa.evidence: 1Point3Acres-sourced report in Ziheng-Qi repo ('his question bank is small'), StaffEngPrep lists 'Expand String', InterviewDB 'Expansion' phone screen last reported ~2026-08; LC-tagged for Stripe.

dsa.title: Store closing-time penalty (Minimum Penalty for a Shop) — 4 parts incl. streaming a huge log
dsa.variant: Part 1: compute_penalty('Y Y N Y', closing_time) (+1 per open hour with no customers, +1 per closed hour with customers). Part 2: find_best_closing_time(log) reusing Part 1. Part 3: an aggregate log mixes many days with BEGIN/END markers and junk ('BEGIN BEGIN N N BEGIN Y Y END N N END'); extract only valid non-nested BEGIN…END segments (can span lines) and return best closing time for each in order. Part 4: same but given a filename too large for memory — stream line by line. Server variant: '0/1' uptime log and 'best removal time'. Tests are expected at each part.
dsa.evidence: Multiple reports (Ziheng-Qi repo with full prompt, 2021 write-up, NodeFlair 'popular'), InterviewDB 'Closing Time' phone screen last reported ~2026-09, FastPrep 7 reports (server variant).

dsa.title: Minimum number of transfers to settle balances (Optimal Account Balancing) — follow-up to account rebalancing
dsa.variant: Appears as the 'algorithmic' follow-up after you write any working set of transfers that brings every account to zero / above a threshold: 'now do it in the minimum number of moves'. Only a verbal approach is expected (greedy max-creditor↔max-debtor, or DFS with pruning; note general optimality is NP-hard). A second follow-up asks how you would audit/verify the transfers in production (invariants, logs, correlation IDs, reconciliation).
dsa.evidence: Stripe's own team-screen prep sample lists it as follow-up 2; reported in 2021 write-up, Ziheng-Qi repo (10, 21), collegesidekick onsite notes, InterviewDB 'Optimizing Money Transfer'.

dsa.title: Card-number range obfuscation (Merge Intervals)
dsa.variant: OA: given card-number ranges [start, end], merge overlapping or adjacent ranges, then obfuscate each endpoint by replacing all digits except the first 2 and last 2 with 'X'; output ascending.
dsa.evidence: Listed among 6 rotating Stripe OA questions (2025); LC 56 is Stripe-tagged in the July 2026 snapshot.

dsa.title: Invalid / suspicious bank transactions in a time window (Invalid Transactions)
dsa.variant: A Feb 2026 technical screen (Chicago, Senior SWE) was described as 'similar to LeetCode Bank transactions, 4 parts of increasing difficulty'; LC 1169 is the most-tagged Stripe problem in the last 6 months. Expect it wrapped as 'flag transactions by same name within 60 min in different cities / over an amount', then extended with new rules per part.
dsa.evidence: Glassdoor Feb 2026 review; LC Stripe tag (6-month window).

dsa.title: Simple Bank System (transfer / deposit / withdraw validity)
dsa.variant: LC-tagged for Stripe; mirrors Part 2 of Stripe's account-balance problem (process transactions in timestamp order and reject any that would make a balance negative). Practise as a warm-up for the practical version.
dsa.evidence: Stripe LC tag only; no direct interview report found.

dsa.title: Windowed alerting on repeated events (Alert Using Same Key-Card Three or More Times in a One Hour Period)
dsa.variant: Same mechanics as Stripe's fraud OA (same user from ≥2 IPs within 10 minutes; >$5000 in any 1-hour window) and the 30-second incident monitor — group by key, sort by parsed time, slide a window.
dsa.evidence: Stripe LC tag; shape matches reported OA fraud problem.

dsa.title: Tiered bracket computation (Calculate Amount Paid in Taxes)
dsa.variant: The bracket logic is exactly what Part 2 of the shipping-cost problem (incremental quantity tiers with null maxQuantity) and Part 3 of transaction fees (volume thresholds) require; practise 'fixed' vs 'incremental' tier semantics and boundary quantities.
dsa.evidence: Stripe LC tag; mechanics reported in shipping-cost and fee problems.

dsa.title: Top K Frequent Elements (asked in JavaScript)
dsa.variant: Reported as 'write a JS function returning the top k most frequent elements' alongside a data-generation/plotting task in a full-stack/data-flavoured loop.
dsa.evidence: One Blind onsite thread.

dsa.title: Next Permutation
dsa.variant: Listed by Prepfully under 'recently reported' Stripe coding questions; an outlier versus the practical style.
dsa.evidence: Prepfully guide only.

dsa.title: Palindromes in base 10 and base k (Sum of k-Mirror Numbers variant)
dsa.variant: Reported as 'first N integers that are palindromes in base 10 and base k' — enumerate base-10 palindromes and test base-k representation.
dsa.evidence: Prepfully 'recently reported'.

dsa.title: Currency arbitrage detection (negative cycle)
dsa.statement: Given exchange-rate triples such as (USD, EUR, 0.90), (EUR, GBP, 0.85), (GBP, USD, 1.35), determine whether a profitable cycle exists (product of rates around a loop > 1). Expected approach: edge weight = -log(rate) and detect a negative cycle with Bellman-Ford; follow-ups ask to output the cycle and the profit factor, and to handle bidirectional/missing rates.
dsa.variant: Natural Part 4 of the currency-conversion problem.
dsa.evidence: Candidate-reported in lhf927 collection.

dsa.title: Deployment window scheduler over a recurring 10,080-minute week
dsa.statement: A week repeats every 10,080 minutes. Teams declare allowed deployment windows and freeze windows, each with a timezone offset; a freeze always wins over an allow. Part 1: normalise windows to UTC minute-of-week and merge them. Part 2: subtract freeze windows (windows may wrap past the week boundary). Part 3: given 'now', a lead time, a minimum slot length and k, return the first k valid UTC deployment windows. Output format is strict.
dsa.variant: OA and screen variants: 'Find Weekly Deployment Windows Across Time Zones', 'Find the First K Valid UTC Deployment Windows'.
dsa.evidence: 1Point3Acres bank has 4 variants (OA post 2026-09-28), PracHub OA 'Hard', InterviewDB 'Deployment' OA ~2026-09, lhf927 collection.

dsa.title: Incident monitor: TRIGGER/RESOLVE alerts over a 30-second sliding window
dsa.statement: Logs arrive sorted as 'timestamp,merchant_id,status_code,count'. Evaluate each log against a 30-second window [T-29, T] per (merchant, error_code). Part 1: emit 'ts,TRIGGER,merchant,code' when ≥5 failures of that code occur in the window, never duplicating while active. Part 2: trigger only if failures are also strictly more than 1% of the merchant's 200-count in the window. Part 3: emit RESOLVE when a new log for that merchant arrives and the condition no longer holds; a pair may re-trigger later. Sort output by ts, merchant, code, event.
dsa.variant: Clarify whether the window lower bound is T-29 or T-30 — the sample output contradicts the text.
dsa.evidence: 1Point3Acres bank (last asked 2026-09-07, OA/phone/tech screen), lhf927 'rolling-window event detection', InterviewDB 'Observability' OA.

dsa.title: Linked merchants / matching contacts by weighted shared attributes (1-hop → 2-hop → component)
dsa.statement: Records come as CSV (id,name,email,company) with a weight per field (e.g. name 0.2, email 0.5, company 0.3) and a threshold (0.5). Two records match if the summed weight of fields that are equal (case-insensitive, trimmed, empty never matches) ≥ threshold. Part 1: ids directly linked to a target. Part 2: records reachable in two hops. Part 3: every record transitively linked (BFS/union-find). Follow-ups: rank by match score, scale with an inverted index per (field,value), float-tolerance pitfalls.
dsa.variant: Also seen as 'New Matching Contacts', 'Six Degrees of Collusion – risk scoring' (OA 'Collusion').
dsa.evidence: PracHub tech screens 2025-12 and 2026-01, 1Point3Acres titles, FastPrep 3 reports (Sep 2026), InterviewDB 'Linked User' (~2026-10) and 'Matching Contacts', Aced guide mentions record deduplication first rounds.

dsa.title: Render a task/subtask hierarchy from unordered flat CSV records
dsa.statement: Records are 'timestamp,task,task_id,name' or 'timestamp,subtask,parent_id,task_id,name' in arbitrary order (children may precede parents). Part 1: build parent→children map and find roots; order roots and siblings by timestamp. Part 2: render as an indented tree with '├─', '└─', '│  ' connectors (exact text compared). Part 3: tolerate malformed lines, duplicate ids, orphans and cycles and report them. Part 4: render only the subtree under a given id. Use an explicit stack (deep chains).
dsa.variant: Reading the long prompt and matching output format consumes most of the hour; many finish only Part 2.
dsa.evidence: 1Point3Acres has three variants (last 2026-09-29), InterviewDB 'Task Tree' phone screen (~2026-10), FastPrep 4 reports Oct 2026, PracHub 'Parse and Format Arbitrarily Nested Tasks from CSV'.

dsa.title: HTTP Accept-Language header parser (4 parts: exact, language-only, wildcard, q-factors)
dsa.statement: parse_accept_language(header, supported) returns supported tags in the client's preference order, with tests. Part 1: exact tags ('en-US, fr-CA, fr-FR' with {fr-FR, en-US} → [en-US, fr-FR]). Part 2: bare language tags ('fr') match every supported regional variant, preserving order and uniqueness ('fr-FR, fr' → fr-FR first, then other fr-*). Part 3: '*' wildcard means all remaining supported languages. Part 4: q-factors ('fr-FR;q=1, fr-CA;q=0, *;q=0.5') — sort by q descending, q=0 means last resort/excluded, ties keep header order.
dsa.variant: OA variant asks only for q-value sorting with default 1.0. Classic since 2021 but still in 2025–26 banks; part 3–4 are rarely finished.
dsa.evidence: Glassdoor (Senior SWE), LeetCode Discuss phone screen, two 1Point3Acres threads, InterviewDB 'Header Parsing' (~2026-04), FastPrep 6 reports (Jan 2025), BigTechExperts.

dsa.title: Card AID parsing with length-prefixed tokens, supported list and RID prefixes
dsa.statement: A string encodes many card application IDs as [2-digit length][AID][2-digit length][AID]… ending with '0', e.g. '18DS012345678987654310AI012345670'. Phase 1: split into the ordered list of AIDs. Phase 2: keep only AIDs present in a supported set, preserving order. Phase 3: a list of RIDs (prefixes) is added — any supported AID starting with a listed RID is also applicable; keep order and uniqueness. You must write your own test cases and ask about malformed input.
dsa.variant: Same skeleton as the Accept-Language problem; the interviewer pasted a batch of hidden tests after Phase 2.
dsa.evidence: US intern phone screen report (Ziheng-Qi repo); InterviewDB 'Card Parsing' phone screen (~2026-09).

dsa.title: Wishlist mutual rankings
dsa.statement: Each user has an ordered wishlist of other users. Step 1: has_mutual_first_choice(user) — do A and B rank each other first; generalise to has_mutual_pair_for_rank(user, rank) and refactor step 1 to use it. Step 2: changed_pairings(user, rank) — which users' mutual status would change if that entry were bumped up one rank. Step 3: anti-pairings counted from the end of each list.
dsa.evidence: 2021 write-up; InterviewDB 'Wishlist' phone screen last reported ~2026-04.

dsa.title: Sticky load balancer simulation with server shutdown (OA)
dsa.statement: Simulate routing long-lived WebSocket connections across m backend servers from a textual sequence of events (connect/disconnect/shutdown). Connections are sticky to their server; new connections go to the least-loaded/round-robin server per the rules; when a server shuts down, its connections are redistributed deterministically. Output the per-event routing or final assignment.
dsa.evidence: PracHub OA entry 'Simulate sticky load balancer with shutdown' (Medium).

dsa.title: Proximity-aware datacenter request router with health management (OA)
dsa.statement: Part 1: register data centers/regions with coordinates. Part 2: route each incoming request (with a location) to the nearest healthy region, with a deterministic tie-break. Part 3: process health updates (mark region unhealthy/healthy) between requests. Part 4: capacity limits or latency weights; report where each request landed and rejected requests.
dsa.evidence: 1Point3Acres OA post 'Proximity Request Routing Challenge' (2026-09-30) plus three bank titles; InterviewDB 'Proximity Request Routing' and 'Request Router' OA (~2026-09).

dsa.title: Fraud detection over time windows (multi-IP in 10 min, >$5000 per hour) — OA
dsa.statement: Given transactions (id, user_id, timestamp, amount, ip), flag a transaction as fraudulent if the same user transacts from more than one IP within any 10-minute window, or if the user's total amount within any 1-hour window exceeds $5000. Return fraudulent transaction ids in ascending order.
dsa.evidence: Listed among rotating Stripe OA questions ('Catch Me If You Can').

dsa.title: Subscription notification timestamps (k-way merge) — OA
dsa.statement: Each subscription has start_time, interval (days) and count. Output the exact timestamps of all notifications across subscriptions sorted by time, breaking ties by subscription id.
dsa.evidence: Rotating OA question list.

dsa.title: Shipping cost packing: greedy → volume constraint → multiple ship types (DP)
dsa.statement: Part 1: pack items into shipments minimising cost — a greedy approach works. Part 2: a volume constraint is added that breaks greedy; you are expected to notice and say so. Part 3: multiple ship types with different cost structures push toward a DP/knapsack formulation.
dsa.variant: Distinct from the shipping-cost tier calculator; about 60 minutes.
dsa.evidence: LeetCode Discuss report summarised in lhf927 collection.

dsa.title: Transaction balancer: contiguous zero-sum groups with non-negative running balance
dsa.statement: Process a list of signed integer transactions sequentially and output every contiguous group whose sum returns to zero, abandoning a group as soon as its running balance goes negative ([2,-2,3,-1,-2,4,-4] → [[2,-2],[3,-1,-2],[4,-4]]). Follow-ups: dollars-and-cents inputs (use integer cents/Decimal, never float), and a streaming version exposed as a class with add(txn).
dsa.evidence: Single candidate document transcribed in Ziheng-Qi repo.

dsa.title: Validate a numeronym
dsa.statement: Given a word and a numeronym like 'i18n' or 'a11y', check that the digits equal the number of omitted letters and the kept letters match; extend to multiple digit groups and case handling.
dsa.evidence: Aced guide 'general coding' examples.

design.title: Ledger / bookkeeping service for a payments platform
design.prompt: Design a bookkeeping service that records money sent and received on behalf of merchants and returns a merchant's balance; define the APIs other Stripe services call (add transaction, get balance, list transactions). Variant: a balance ledger that sustains very high write throughput for a single hot merchant without becoming a bottleneck; variant: a scalable idempotent ledger service.
probes: double-entry model and immutability (corrections via reversing entries)
idempotent writes / dedupe under retries and concurrent duplicates
balance read path: materialised balance vs summing postings, and what to do when they disagree
hot-account contention (platform fee account touched by every transfer) without breaking zero-sum
sharding and cross-shard transfers; recovering a prepared-but-uncommitted transfer
as-of-time balance queries, retention, audit trail

Stage 2: when no invoice id is given, match by exact amount and prefer the earliest due date. Stage 3: a forgiveness/tolerance value is supplied — invoices within ±tolerance of the amount qualify (exact match still wins), choose the earliest and report the forgiven amount. Occasionally Stage 4: partial payments / several payments against one invoice.

Stage 2: a list of plan changes {name, new_plan, change_date} adds a 'Changed' email and later emails must reference the new plan. Stage 3 (bonus): renewals {name, extension, change_date} push the expiry out and re-emit the upcoming/expired emails. Variant A: a send_schedule map {'start': 'Welcome', '-15': 'Starting soon', '60': 'How is it going?', 'end': 'Goodbye'} where numeric keys are minute offsets from start — return who gets which email at a given 'now' without hard-coding offsets. Variant B: an Invoicer class built from {offset → template}; send_emails(invoices) returns reminders sorted by time; follow-up adds payments that cancel pending reminders.
